title: Portuguese capture of Goa
summary: Afonso de Albuquerque takes Goa from the Bijapur sultanate on his second attempt of the year.
whyItMatters: Goa became the seat of the Portuguese Estado da Índia and stayed under Portuguese rule until 1961.
evidenceNote: Portuguese dispatches and Deccan chronicles agree on the capture and its date (St Catherine’s Day).

title: First Battle of Panipat
summary: Babur defeats and kills Sultan Ibrahim Lodi, using field artillery and wagon barricades.
whyItMatters: Ends the Delhi Sultanate’s Lodi dynasty and opens Mughal rule in Hindustan.
evidenceNote: Described at first hand by Babur; the outcome is confirmed by Afghan and later Mughal histories. Army sizes rest on Babur’s own estimates.

title: Battle of Khanwa
summary: Babur defeats the Rajput confederacy led by Rana Sanga of Mewar.
whyItMatters: Secures Babur’s hold on Agra and Delhi against the strongest rival coalition.
evidenceNote: Babur’s memoir is the main narrative. Some works give 16 March.

title: Battle of Chausa
summary: Sher Khan Sur surprises Humayun’s camp at dawn; Humayun escapes across the Ganga.
whyItMatters: Sher Khan takes the title Sher Shah and Mughal power in the east collapses.
evidenceNote: Reported by both Afghan and Mughal traditions, each written decades later.

title: Battle of Kannauj (Bilgram)
summary: Sher Shah routs Humayun a second time; Humayun flees toward Sindh and then Persia.
whyItMatters: Begins fifteen years of Sur rule and Humayun’s exile.
evidenceNote: Both traditions agree on the outcome and the date.

title: Accession of Akbar
summary: Thirteen-year-old Akbar is proclaimed emperor on a brick platform at Kalanaur after Humayun’s death; Bairam Khan acts as regent.
whyItMatters: Starts a reign of almost fifty years that consolidated the empire.
evidenceNote: Recorded in the Akbarnāma; the enthronement platform survives at the site.

title: Second Battle of Panipat
summary: Akbar’s army under Bairam Khan defeats Hemu, who is struck in the eye by an arrow and captured.
whyItMatters: Recovers Delhi and Agra for the Mughals.
evidenceNote: Accounts differ on who killed the captured Hemu — Akbar himself or Bairam Khan.

title: Battle of Talikota
summary: The allied Deccan sultanates defeat Vijayanagara; Rama Raya is captured and beheaded, and the capital is sacked.
whyItMatters: Breaks Vijayanagara as the dominant power of the south.
evidenceNote: The outcome is certain. The exact field and the date are not: the fighting was some distance from Talikota itself, and sources give 23 or 26 January.

title: Fall of Chittorgarh
summary: After a siege of about four months Akbar takes the Mewar fortress; the garrison’s commander Jaimal is killed.
whyItMatters: Removes the principal Rajput stronghold resisting Mughal expansion.
evidenceNote: Mughal chronicles describe the siege in detail; casualty figures are theirs alone.

title: Founding of Fatehpur Sikri
summary: Akbar begins a new capital beside the hospice of Shaikh Salim Chishti.
whyItMatters: Served as the imperial capital for roughly fourteen years; the complex survives largely intact.
evidenceNote: Chronicles and the standing buildings agree; the start of construction is known to the year.

title: Battle of Haldighati
summary: A Mughal army under Man Singh of Amber fights Maharana Pratap of Mewar; Pratap withdraws into the hills and continues resistance.
whyItMatters: A tactical Mughal success that failed to end Mewar’s independence.
evidenceNote: Badaʾuni fought in the battle and describes it. Some works give 21 June; the size of both armies is debated.

title: Execution of Guru Arjan
summary: Guru Arjan, fifth Sikh Guru, dies in Mughal custody at Lahore after Jahangir orders his punishment.
whyItMatters: A turning point in Sikh–Mughal relations.
evidenceNote: Jahangir’s memoir records the order. The manner of death is known from Sikh tradition and a Jesuit letter, which differ in detail.

title: Thomas Roe’s first audience with Jahangir
summary: The English ambassador is received by Jahangir at the court then resident in Ajmer.
whyItMatters: Opens three years of negotiation over English trading rights.
evidenceNote: Known from Roe’s own journal; Jahangir’s memoir does not mention him.

title: Death of Mumtaz Mahal
summary: Mumtaz Mahal dies in childbirth while accompanying Shah Jahan on campaign in the Deccan.
whyItMatters: Her tomb at Agra, the Taj Mahal, was begun the following year.
evidenceNote: Recorded by Shah Jahan’s court chroniclers.

title: Construction of the Taj Mahal begins
summary: Work starts on the mausoleum of Mumtaz Mahal on the bank of the Yamuna.
whyItMatters: The mausoleum was substantially complete by 1643 and the whole complex about a decade later.
evidenceNote: Court chronicles, a European visitor (Peter Mundy, 1632–33) and inscriptions on the building agree on the chronology.

title: Birth of Shivaji
summary: Shivaji is born to Jijabai and Shahaji Bhonsle at the hill fort of Shivneri near Junnar.
whyItMatters: Founder of the Maratha kingdom.
evidenceNote: The Jedhe chronology gives a date equal to 19 February 1630, now the accepted one. Older bakhars give 1627.

title: Grant of Madraspatnam to the English
summary: Francis Day obtains a grant of a strip of coast from the local nayak; Fort St George is begun the next year.
whyItMatters: The first substantial English territorial foothold in India.
evidenceNote: The grant survives in Company records.

title: Shahjahanabad inaugurated
summary: Shah Jahan formally enters his new walled capital and its palace-fortress, the Red Fort, begun in 1639.
whyItMatters: Returns the imperial capital from Agra to Delhi.
evidenceNote: Court chronicles give the ceremony; the buildings stand.

title: Battle of Samugarh
summary: Aurangzeb and Murad defeat their elder brother Dara Shikoh in the decisive battle of the succession war.
whyItMatters: Aurangzeb takes Agra, confines Shah Jahan and assumes the throne.
evidenceNote: Described by court historians and by the European eyewitnesses Bernier and Manucci. Works using New Style give 8 June.

title: Meeting at Pratapgad
summary: Shivaji kills the Bijapur general Afzal Khan at a parley below the fort; Maratha forces then rout the Bijapur army.
whyItMatters: Establishes Shivaji as a regional power.
evidenceNote: That Afzal Khan was killed at the meeting is certain. Who struck first is disputed between Maratha and Bijapur-side accounts.

title: Night raid on Shaista Khan
summary: Shivaji leads a small party into the Mughal viceroy’s residence at Pune; Shaista Khan is wounded and loses a son.
whyItMatters: Aurangzeb transfers Shaista Khan to Bengal; Mughal prestige in the Deccan suffers.
evidenceNote: Reported by Maratha, Mughal and English factory sources; the size of the raiding party varies between them.

title: Sack of Surat
summary: Shivaji’s cavalry enters the Mughal empire’s richest port and plunders it for several days; the English and Dutch factories hold out.
whyItMatters: Shows that Mughal revenue centres were within Maratha reach.
evidenceNote: Described day by day in English and Dutch factory correspondence written during the raid.

title: Treaty of Purandar
summary: Besieged by Mirza Raja Jai Singh, Shivaji agrees to surrender 23 forts and to serve the empire.
whyItMatters: Leads directly to his journey to the imperial court the following year.
evidenceNote: Terms are known from Jai Singh’s own dispatches as well as Maratha accounts.

title: Shivaji’s audience with Aurangzeb
summary: Presented at court on the emperor’s birthday, Shivaji is placed among commanders of 5,000, protests the slight aloud and leaves the line. He is then kept under guard in Agra.
whyItMatters: The breach ends the Purandar settlement and sets up his escape and the renewed war.
evidenceNote: Reported within days by letters from Ram Singh’s camp and by the court record. The words spoken are not preserved.

title: Escape from Agra
summary: Shivaji and his son Sambhaji slip out of guarded quarters; the absence is discovered the next day.
whyItMatters: He reaches Rajgad later in the year and rebuilds his position.
evidenceNote: The escape and its date are firm. The method — hiding in baskets sent out as alms — comes from later narratives, and the route home is not securely known.

title: Recapture of Sinhagad
summary: A night escalade led by Tanaji Malusare retakes the fort from its Mughal garrison; Tanaji is killed.
whyItMatters: Opens Shivaji’s recovery of the forts ceded at Purandar.
evidenceNote: The capture is dated by the Jedhe chronology. Much popular detail derives from a later ballad.

title: Battle of Saraighat
summary: The Ahom army under Lachit Borphukan defeats a Mughal force led by Ram Singh of Amber in a river battle on the Brahmaputra.
whyItMatters: Ends the last major Mughal attempt to hold Assam.
evidenceNote: Ahom buranjis and Mughal sources agree on the outcome; it is dated to the year here.

title: Coronation of Shivaji
summary: Shivaji is crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad with rites conducted by Gaga Bhatt of Varanasi.
whyItMatters: Declares a sovereign Maratha kingdom.
evidenceNote: Witnessed by the English envoy Henry Oxinden, whose narrative survives, and recorded in Maratha sources.

title: Death of Shivaji
summary: Shivaji dies at Raigad after a short illness.
whyItMatters: A succession dispute follows; Aurangzeb moves to the Deccan in person the next year.
evidenceNote: The date is firm. The nature of the illness is described differently by different sources.

title: Job Charnock settles at Sutanuti
summary: The English East India Company’s agent returns to the Hooghly and establishes the settlement that grew into Calcutta.
whyItMatters: Later the capital of British India.
evidenceNote: Recorded in the Company’s own diary. Whether this counts as the “founding” of the city is a matter of interpretation.

title: Creation of the Khalsa
summary: At the Vaisakhi gathering Guru Gobind Singh initiates the first five members of the Khalsa.
whyItMatters: Gives the Sikh community its distinct initiated order.
evidenceNote: The founding is firm; the earliest written narratives of the ceremony are from the following decades. Vaisakhi 1699 fell on 30 March Old Style; the date is often cited as 13 April.

title: Death of Aurangzeb
summary: Aurangzeb dies in camp after a quarter-century of campaigning in the Deccan; he is buried at Khuldabad.
whyItMatters: A war of succession follows and imperial authority fragments over the next decades.
evidenceNote: Recorded by court chroniclers. 3 March is New Style (20 February Old Style).

title: Battle of Palkhed
summary: Peshwa Baji Rao I outmanoeuvres the Nizam of Hyderabad, cuts his supplies and forces terms.
whyItMatters: The Nizam recognises Maratha claims to revenue in the Deccan.
evidenceNote: The campaign ended in the Nizam’s encirclement rather than a pitched battle; the settlement followed days later.

title: Battle of Karnal
summary: Nadir Shah of Iran defeats the army of the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah in a few hours, then occupies and plunders Delhi.
whyItMatters: The Peacock Throne and the imperial treasury are carried off; Mughal power never recovers.
evidenceNote: Described by Persian and Indian chroniclers on both sides. 24 February is New Style.

title: Battle of Plassey
summary: Robert Clive’s Company force defeats Nawab Siraj-ud-Daula after Mir Jafar’s division stands aside.
whyItMatters: Makes the East India Company the controlling power in Bengal.
evidenceNote: Clive’s dispatches, Orme’s history and Persian accounts agree on the course of the day.

title: Battle of Wandiwash
summary: Eyre Coote defeats the French under the Comte de Lally.
whyItMatters: Ends French prospects of empire in India; Pondicherry falls a year later.
evidenceNote: British and French participants’ accounts survive.

title: Third Battle of Panipat
summary: Ahmad Shah Durrani and his Indian allies destroy the Maratha army commanded by Sadashivrao Bhau.
whyItMatters: Halts Maratha expansion in the north for a decade.
evidenceNote: Kashiraj Pandit’s eyewitness account is the fullest narrative. Casualty totals are estimates and vary widely.

title: Battle of Buxar
summary: Hector Munro’s Company army defeats the combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh and the emperor Shah Alam II.
whyItMatters: Confirms Company supremacy in the east and leads to the grant of the diwani.
evidenceNote: Some works date the battle 23 October.

title: Treaty of Allahabad
summary: Shah Alam II grants the East India Company the diwani — the right to collect revenue — of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
whyItMatters: Turns a trading company into a territorial government.
evidenceNote: The treaty and the imperial grant survive; the grant itself is dated 12 August.

title: Fall of Srirangapatna
summary: Company forces storm the island capital of Mysore; Tipu Sultan is killed defending a gateway.
whyItMatters: Ends the Anglo-Mysore wars; Mysore becomes a subsidiary state.
evidenceNote: Described by several officers present, including Beatson.

title: Battle of the Hydaspes
summary: Alexander of Macedon defeats King Porus on the Jhelum, then turns back at the Beas.
whyItMatters: The furthest point of Alexander’s advance into India.
evidenceNote: Known from Greek and Roman histories written centuries later from lost eyewitness accounts. The exact battlefield is not identified.

title: Chandragupta Maurya takes Pataliputra
summary: Chandragupta overthrows the Nanda dynasty and founds the Maurya empire.
whyItMatters: The first empire to unite most of the subcontinent.
evidenceNote: The date is approximate; estimates range from about 324 to 320 BCE.

title: Kalinga War
summary: Ashoka conquers Kalinga with great loss of life and afterwards turns to the policy he calls dhamma.
whyItMatters: Recorded by Ashoka himself as the cause of his change of course.
evidenceNote: Ashoka’s Rock Edict XIII describes the war and his remorse. The date follows from his regnal years and is approximate.

title: Accession of Chandragupta I
summary: Chandragupta I takes the imperial title; the Gupta era is counted from about this year.
whyItMatters: Opens the Gupta period.
evidenceNote: Deduced from the starting point of the Gupta era used in later inscriptions.

title: Harsha’s assembly at Kannauj
summary: Harsha convenes a great assembly of rulers and scholars, at which the pilgrim Xuanzang is honoured.
whyItMatters: The fullest contemporary picture of a north Indian court of the seventh century.
evidenceNote: Described by Xuanzang, who was present; no Indian account of the assembly survives.

title: Arab conquest of Sindh
summary: Muhammad bin Qasim defeats Raja Dahir and brings Sindh under the Umayyad Caliphate.
whyItMatters: The first lasting Muslim rule in the subcontinent.
evidenceNote: The fullest narrative, the Chachnama, is a thirteenth-century Persian version of an earlier Arabic account.

title: Battle of Peshawar
summary: Mahmud of Ghazni defeats the Hindu Shahi king Jayapala.
whyItMatters: Opens Mahmud’s series of campaigns into India.
evidenceNote: Reported by Ghaznavid court historians.

title: Brihadisvara temple completed
summary: Rajaraja I completes the great temple at his capital.
whyItMatters: The largest temple of its age in India; its walls carry the fullest inscriptions of Chola administration.
evidenceNote: Dated by the temple’s own inscriptions to the king’s twenty-fifth regnal year.

title: Mahmud of Ghazni sacks Somnath
summary: Mahmud’s army takes and plunders the temple town of Somnath.
whyItMatters: The most remembered of his raids, in both Persian and later Indian tradition.
evidenceNote: Described by Ghaznavid-era authors; later accounts add much that the earliest do not contain.

title: Second Battle of Tarain
summary: Muhammad of Ghor defeats Prithviraj Chauhan, a year after losing to him on the same ground.
whyItMatters: Opens northern India to the Ghurids and, after them, the Delhi Sultanate.
evidenceNote: Told by Minhaj from Ghurid informants; the Rajput tradition survives only in a much later epic.

title: Qutb al-Din Aibak becomes sultan
summary: On the death of Muhammad of Ghor, his general Aibak assumes independent rule in India.
whyItMatters: Counted as the foundation of the Delhi Sultanate.
evidenceNote: Recorded by Minhaj. Aibak ruled from Lahore; Delhi became the capital under Iltutmish.

title: Alauddin Khalji takes Chittor
summary: The fortress falls to the Delhi sultan after a siege of about eight months.
whyItMatters: Brings Mewar’s chief stronghold under Delhi for a generation.
evidenceNote: Described by Amir Khusrau, who accompanied the army. The story of Padmini first appears more than two centuries later.

title: Capital moved to Daulatabad
summary: Muhammad bin Tughluq orders the court, and much of Delhi’s elite, to move 1,100 km south.
whyItMatters: An attempt to rule the Deccan from within it; abandoned within a decade.
evidenceNote: Barani and Ibn Battuta both describe it, and disagree on how far Delhi was emptied.

title: Founding of Vijayanagara
summary: Harihara and Bukka establish a kingdom on the Tungabhadra.
whyItMatters: Grew into the dominant power of the south for two centuries.
evidenceNote: The year 1336 is traditional. The founders’ origins are debated, and the earliest inscriptions are a little later.

title: Bahmani Sultanate founded
summary: Deccan nobles in revolt against Delhi enthrone Hasan Gangu as Alauddin Bahman Shah.
whyItMatters: The first independent Muslim kingdom of the Deccan.
evidenceNote: Told by Firishta two and a half centuries later from earlier chronicles.

title: Timur sacks Delhi
summary: Timur defeats Sultan Mahmud Tughluq outside Delhi; the city is plundered for days.
whyItMatters: The Sultanate never recovers its former extent.
evidenceNote: Recorded in Timur’s court histories and in Indian chronicles.

title: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut
summary: A Portuguese fleet anchors off the Malabar coast after rounding Africa.
whyItMatters: Opens the direct sea route between Europe and India.
evidenceNote: Described in a journal kept by a member of the fleet.

title: Battle of Koregaon
summary: A small Company force holds a village on the Bhima against the Peshwa’s army for a day.
whyItMatters: Part of the war that ended the Peshwa’s rule within months.
evidenceNote: Reported in Company dispatches; Maratha accounts are sparse.

title: Annexation of the Punjab
summary: After the Second Anglo-Sikh War the Sikh kingdom is annexed by the East India Company.
whyItMatters: Completes Company control of the plains of northern India.
evidenceNote: The terms were signed at Lahore and survive.

title: Outbreak at Meerut
summary: Sepoys of the Bengal Army rise against their officers and march on Delhi.
whyItMatters: Start of the great rebellion of 1857.
evidenceNote: Reported by participants on both sides and in the later trial records.

title: Queen’s Proclamation
summary: The proclamation transferring the government of India from the Company to the Crown is read out.
whyItMatters: Formal beginning of the British Raj.
evidenceNote: The text survives.

title: First session of the Indian National Congress
summary: Seventy-two delegates meet at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College.
whyItMatters: Founding of the organisation that led the independence movement.
evidenceNote: The proceedings were printed.

title: Partition of Bengal
summary: Bengal is divided into two provinces; the day is marked by a general strike and the tying of rakhis.
whyItMatters: Sets off the Swadeshi movement. The partition was annulled in 1911.
evidenceNote: Government orders and the contemporary press.

title: Delhi Durbar
summary: George V announces the transfer of the capital from Calcutta to Delhi and the reunification of Bengal.
whyItMatters: Delhi becomes the capital of British India.
evidenceNote: Official record of the proceedings.

title: Jallianwala Bagh massacre
summary: Troops under Brigadier-General Dyer fire on an unarmed crowd in an enclosed garden.
whyItMatters: A turning point in Indian opinion of British rule.
evidenceNote: The event is documented by the official Hunter Committee and a Congress inquiry. The death toll is disputed: 379 officially, about 1,000 by the Congress count.

title: Salt March reaches Dandi
summary: Gandhi picks up salt on the shore, breaking the salt law after a march of 24 days.
whyItMatters: Launches the Civil Disobedience movement.
evidenceNote: Reported day by day in the press and in Gandhi’s own writings.

title: Quit India resolution
summary: The All-India Congress Committee calls for an immediate end to British rule; its leaders are arrested the next morning.
whyItMatters: The last mass movement before independence.
evidenceNote: The resolution and speeches were published.

title: Independence of India
summary: Power is transferred at midnight; British India is partitioned into India and Pakistan.
whyItMatters: End of British rule. Partition displaced many millions.
evidenceNote: Recorded in the Constituent Assembly debates and the Indian Independence Act.

title: Assassination of Mahatma Gandhi
summary: Gandhi is shot on his way to an evening prayer meeting at Birla House.
whyItMatters: Removed the movement’s central figure months after independence.
evidenceNote: Established at the trial that followed; the time of 5:17pm is widely and consistently cited.

title: Constitution of India comes into force
summary: India becomes a republic.
whyItMatters: The founding law of the Republic of India.
evidenceNote: The Constitution itself.

title: Surrender at Dhaka
summary: Pakistani forces in the east surrender to the joint Indian and Bangladeshi command.
whyItMatters: Ends the war of 1971; Bangladesh becomes independent.
evidenceNote: The instrument of surrender survives.

title: First nuclear test at Pokhran
summary: India carries out an underground nuclear explosion in the Rajasthan desert.
whyItMatters: India becomes the sixth country to test a nuclear device.
evidenceNote: Announced by the Government of India the same day.

title: Chandrayaan-3 lands on the Moon
summary: The Vikram lander touches down near the lunar south pole.
whyItMatters: India becomes the fourth country to land softly on the Moon and the first near its south pole.
evidenceNote: Announced and broadcast by ISRO. The place shown is the mission control centre.

title: Operation Blue Star
summary: The Indian Army storms the Golden Temple complex at Amritsar to remove armed militants led by Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale.
whyItMatters: Deeply alienated many Sikhs and led directly to Indira Gandhi's assassination that October.
evidenceNote: The main assault ran 3-6 June 1984; the single date given here marks its start.

title: Assassination of Indira Gandhi
summary: Indira Gandhi is shot by two of her own Sikh bodyguards at her residence, in apparent retaliation for Operation Blue Star.
whyItMatters: Triggered anti-Sikh riots across India and brought Rajiv Gandhi to power the same day.
evidenceNote: The time of approximately 9:20am is widely and consistently cited.

title: Stand at Pavan Khind
summary: Baji Prabhu Deshpande holds the narrow pass with a small rearguard, covering Shivaji's retreat from the siege of Panhala to Vishalgad, and dies in the fighting once word reaches him that Shivaji is safe.
whyItMatters: Preserves Shivaji and the core of his forces at a moment the Panhala garrison could otherwise have been destroyed; the pass is named Pavan Khind ("sacred pass") for the stand.
evidenceNote: The stand and Baji Prabhu's death are consistently recorded across the Maratha bakhars; the exact strength of the rearguard varies between accounts.

title: Treaty of Amritsar
summary: The British sell Kashmir to Gulab Singh for 7.5 million rupees, founding the Dogra princely state of Jammu and Kashmir.
whyItMatters: Creates the princely state whose later accession dispute shapes the modern Kashmir conflict.
evidenceNote: The date is well attested, though one source gives 15 March.

title: Battle of Khajwa
summary: Aurangzeb's forces defeat Shah Shuja, the last major battle of the Mughal war of succession.
whyItMatters: Secures Aurangzeb's throne after his victories over Dara Shikoh.
evidenceNote: Date well attested; one secondary source misdates it to 1658.

title: Founding of Jodhpur
summary: Rao Jodha founds Mehrangarh fort and the city of Jodhpur as the new Rathore capital of Marwar.
whyItMatters: Jodhpur remains the Rathore capital for the rest of the Marwar state’s history.
evidenceNote: Date still kept as Jodhpur’s annual foundation day.

title: Battle of Raichur
summary: Krishnadevaraya defeats the Bijapur Sultanate under Ismail Adil Shah after a three-month siege, taking the fortress of Raichur.
whyItMatters: One of Vijayanagara’s greatest military victories, securing the Krishna-Tungabhadra doab.
evidenceNote: One source gives 20 May for the main clash.

title: Death of Jaswant Singh Rathore
summary: Jaswant Singh, Maharaja of Marwar and Mughal general, dies at Jamrud near the Khyber Pass.
whyItMatters: His death without an heir acknowledged by the Mughal court triggers the Rathore rebellion.
evidenceNote: One source gives November 1678 instead.

title: Nawab of Junagadh signs accession to Pakistan
summary: Nawab Mahabat Khanji III signs an Instrument of Accession to Pakistan, a decision overturned months later after popular unrest and Indian intervention.
whyItMatters: Becomes one of the first and most contested princely-state accession disputes of Partition.
evidenceNote: Sources differ on which date marks the "accession": the Nawab’s 15 August public announcement, this 14 September signing, or Pakistan’s 16 September acceptance.

title: Bahawalpur accedes to Pakistan
summary: Nawab Sadeq Mohammad Khan V signs an agreement acceding Bahawalpur State to Pakistan.
whyItMatters: One of the largest princely states to join Pakistan at independence.
evidenceNote: Accession accepted by Pakistan on 9 October; some sources give 7 October for the state capital’s own account.

title: Founding of the Khalsa
summary: Guru Gobind Singh calls Sikhs to Anandpur for Vaisakhi, initiates the Panj Piare, and founds the Khalsa order.
whyItMatters: Establishes the Khalsa identity and initiation ceremony still followed by Sikhs today.
evidenceNote: The year and festival are firmly fixed; the precise Gregorian equivalent of the traditional date varies slightly by source.

title: Death of Sher Shah Suri
summary: Sher Shah Suri dies from an accidental gunpowder explosion during his siege of the fort of Kalinjar, just as it is about to fall.
whyItMatters: Ends the reign of the Sur Empire’s founder and ablest ruler.
evidenceNote: Accounts differ on the exact mechanism of the explosion.

title: Ranjit Singh takes Lahore
summary: Ranjit Singh, chief of the Sukerchakia Misl, enters Lahore through the Lohari Gate and becomes master of the city.
whyItMatters: Lays the foundation of the Sikh Empire, with Lahore as its capital.

title: Death of Ranjit Singh
summary: Maharaja Ranjit Singh dies at Lahore after a series of strokes.
whyItMatters: His death opens a succession crisis that leads to the Sikh Empire’s fragmentation within a decade.

title: Death of Guru Gobind Singh
summary: Guru Gobind Singh dies at Nanded from wounds inflicted by assassins sent by Wazir Khan, after naming the Guru Granth Sahib his successor.
whyItMatters: Ends the line of living Sikh Gurus.
evidenceNote: One source gives 6 October, likely reflecting the Guruship transfer rather than the death itself.

title: Battle of Nesari
summary: Prataprao Gujar and six companions charge a vastly larger Bijapur force under Bahlol Khan and are killed.
whyItMatters: One of the most celebrated acts of sacrifice in early Maratha military history.

title: Death of Balaji Baji Rao
summary: Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao dies at Parvati Hill, Pune, five months after the catastrophic Maratha defeat at Panipat.
whyItMatters: His death, following so soon after Panipat, marks the end of an era of unchecked Maratha expansion.

title: Birth of Mohandas Gandhi
summary: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi is born at Porbandar in Gujarat.
whyItMatters: Birth of the figure who would lead India’s independence movement.

title: Birth of Jawaharlal Nehru
summary: Jawaharlal Nehru is born at Allahabad into the prominent Nehru family.
whyItMatters: Birth of India’s first prime minister.

title: Birth of Muhammad Ali Jinnah
summary: Muhammad Ali Jinnah is born at Karachi.
whyItMatters: Birth of the founder and first Governor-General of Pakistan.

title: First Battle of Tarain
summary: Prithviraj Chauhan defeats the invading Ghurid army under Muhammad of Ghor, who is wounded and retreats.
whyItMatters: A rare Rajput victory that delays the Ghurid conquest of northern India by a year.
evidenceNote: Told mainly from the Ghurid side by Minhaj; the Rajput account survives only in later epic tradition.

title: Alauddin Khalji's conquest of Ranthambore
summary: Alauddin Khalji captures Ranthambore fort after a prolonged siege; the Chahamana ruler Hammiradeva dies in the final assault.
whyItMatters: Removes a major Rajput stronghold that had sheltered rebels against Delhi.

title: Alauddin Khalji enthroned at Delhi
summary: Alauddin Khalji is formally enthroned as Sultan of Delhi, months after killing his uncle Jalaluddin Khalji at Kara.
whyItMatters: Begins the reign of the Khalji dynasty’s most powerful sultan.
evidenceNote: His reign is sometimes dated from the July 1296 killing of Jalaluddin at Kara instead.

title: Execution of Dara Shikoh
summary: Dara Shikoh is executed on Aurangzeb’s order on a charge of apostasy, after being paraded in chains through Delhi.
whyItMatters: Removes Aurangzeb’s last serious rival for the Mughal throne.

title: Death of Hyder Ali
summary: Hyder Ali dies of a tumor at his camp near Chittoor during the Second Anglo-Mysore War.
whyItMatters: His son Tipu Sultan succeeds him and continues the war against the British.

title: Death of Rajaram
summary: Chhatrapati Rajaram dies of illness at Sinhagad fort, where he had taken refuge during a Mughal raid on Satara.
whyItMatters: His widow Tarabai takes up the regency for their infant son, continuing Maratha resistance to the Mughals.

title: Reported death of Subhas Chandra Bose
summary: Subhas Chandra Bose dies of burns, by the official account, after his overloaded bomber crashes on takeoff at Taihoku airfield.
whyItMatters: Ends the life of the Indian National Army’s leader; the manner of his death remained disputed in India for decades.
evidenceNote: Three Indian government inquiries reached different conclusions; the Shah Nawaz (1956) and Khosla (1970) commissions accepted the crash account, while the Mukherjee Commission (2005) did not.

title: Constitution of India adopted
summary: The Constituent Assembly adopts the Constitution of India, which comes into force on 26 January 1950.
whyItMatters: B. R. Ambedkar, as chairman of the Drafting Committee, is its principal architect.

title: Operation Polo: annexation of Hyderabad
summary: The Indian Army's five-day operation ends with the Nizam of Hyderabad ordering a ceasefire; state forces formally surrender the next day.
whyItMatters: Integrates the largest princely state that had not acceded to India, directed on the Indian side by Sardar Patel.
evidenceNote: The operation ran 13-18 September 1948; 17 September (the ceasefire) is commemorated as Hyderabad Liberation Day.

title: Accession of Maharana Pratap
summary: Pratap Singh is crowned Maharana of Mewar at Gogunda.
whyItMatters: Begins the reign that would resist Akbar’s expansion for the next 25 years.

title: Death of Maharana Pratap
summary: Maharana Pratap dies at Chavand from injuries suffered in a hunting accident.
whyItMatters: Ends the reign of Mewar’s most celebrated resister of Mughal authority.
evidenceNote: One source gives 29 January instead.

title: Battle of Chamkaur
summary: Guru Gobind Singh and a small band hold off a vastly larger Mughal and hill-chief force at Chamkaur; his two eldest sons, Sahibzada Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh’s older brothers, die in the fighting.
whyItMatters: One of the most commemorated last stands in Sikh history.
evidenceNote: Sources give dates ranging from 6 to 23 December 1704, and some place it in 1705; 7 December reflects Pal Singh Purewal’s correction of an earlier Bikrami-calendar conversion.

title: Martyrdom of Guru Gobind Singh’s younger sons
summary: Guru Gobind Singh's two youngest sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, are executed at Sirhind on the order of the Mughal governor Wazir Khan after refusing to convert to Islam.
whyItMatters: Among the most solemnly commemorated martyrdoms in Sikh history.

title: Capture of Sambhaji
summary: A Mughal raiding party under Muqarrab Khan, guided by the defector Ganoji Shirke, surprises and captures Sambhaji and his adviser Kavi Kalash at Sangameshwar.
whyItMatters: Leads directly to his execution six weeks later.

title: Execution of Sambhaji
summary: Sambhaji and Kavi Kalash are executed on Aurangzeb’s order at Tulapur after weeks of captivity and torture.
whyItMatters: Removes the second Maratha Chhatrapati but fails to end Maratha resistance.

title: Assassination of Muhammad of Ghor
summary: Muhammad of Ghor is assassinated near the Jhelum while returning from his campaign against the Khokhars, traditionally blamed on Isma’ili emissaries or Khokhar avengers.
whyItMatters: Leaves his Indian conquests to his viceroy Qutb al-Din Aibak, who founds the Delhi Sultanate.
evidenceNote: Early Persian chroniclers and later accounts blaming the Khokhars disagree on the killers’ identity.

title: Treaty of Madras
summary: Hyder Ali and the East India Company sign the Treaty of Madras, ending the First Anglo-Mysore War on terms of mutual restitution.
whyItMatters: The Company’s only Anglo-Mysore War that ends without territorial loss to Mysore.

title: Execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur
summary: Guru Tegh Bahadur is publicly beheaded at Chandni Chowk on Aurangzeb’s order after refusing to convert to Islam.
whyItMatters: A foundational martyrdom in Sikh history, commemorated annually.
evidenceNote: The Nanakshahi calendar observes the anniversary on 24 November instead, a different calendar conversion of the same event.

title: Assassination of Rajiv Gandhi
summary: Rajiv Gandhi is killed by a suicide bomber of the LTTE while campaigning at Sriperumbudur, Tamil Nadu.
whyItMatters: The second assassination of an Indian prime minister, during the 1991 general election.

title: The Emergency is proclaimed
summary: On Indira Gandhi's advice, President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed proclaims a state of national emergency under Article 352, suspending civil liberties.
whyItMatters: Begins 21 months of authoritarian rule, among the most consequential and controversial periods in independent India’s history.
evidenceNote: Signed just before midnight; many citizens learned of it only the next morning, and Gandhi’s own radio address came on 26 June.

title: Assassination of Pilaji Gaekwad
summary: Pilaji Gaekwad is assassinated at Dakor on the order of Abhai Singh, the Mughal governor of Gujarat.
whyItMatters: His son Damaji Rao Gaekwad succeeds him, continuing the Gaekwad rise to control of Baroda.

title: Mangal Pandey’s mutiny at Barrackpore
summary: Sepoy Mangal Pandey attacks his officers on the parade ground over the greased-cartridge controversy, the first major incident of the uprising.
whyItMatters: Widely regarded as the spark that lit the wider Indian Rebellion of 1857.

title: Capture of Kanpur and the Bibighar massacre
summary: Nana Sahib’s forces capture Kanpur; British women and children held captive at the Bibighar are massacred.
whyItMatters: One of the most notorious episodes of the revolt on either side, hardening British reprisals.

title: Siege of Jhansi
summary: General Hugh Rose's Central India Field Force storms Jhansi after a siege begun 24 March; Rani Lakshmibai escapes as the city falls.
whyItMatters: One of the decisive campaigns of the revolt’s suppression in central India.
evidenceNote: The siege ran from 24 March; the town was stormed 3 April and the fort occupied 5 April.

title: Battle of the Betwa
summary: Hugh Rose's force defeats Tantia Tope's larger relief army near the Betwa river during the siege of Jhansi.
whyItMatters: Removes the last hope of relief for besieged Jhansi.
evidenceNote: Sources differ between 31 March and 1 April.

title: Death of Rani Lakshmibai at Kotah-ki-Serai
summary: Rani Lakshmibai is killed in battle against British cavalry near Gwalior.
whyItMatters: Her death and the manner of it made her one of the revolt’s most enduringly celebrated figures.
evidenceNote: 18 June is popularly observed as her anniversary; contemporary military records favor 17 June.

title: Execution of Tantia Tope
summary: Tantia Tope is hanged at Shivpuri after a court-martial, having been betrayed and captured in the Paron forest.
whyItMatters: Removes the last major rebel military leader still in the field, effectively ending organized resistance.

title: Trial and conviction of Bahadur Shah II
summary: Bahadur Shah II is tried and found guilty of rebellion and complicity in the killing of Europeans during the 1857 revolt.
whyItMatters: Ends any claim to real Mughal authority and leads directly to his exile.
evidenceNote: Sources vary on the trial’s exact span (January-April 1858); 29 March is the most specific conviction date found.

title: Death of Lala Lajpat Rai
summary: Lala Lajpat Rai dies from injuries sustained eighteen days earlier when police baton-charged the march he led against the Simon Commission.
whyItMatters: His death directly motivates the assassination of John Saunders three weeks later.

title: Assassination of John Saunders
summary: Bhagat Singh and Rajguru shoot and kill police officer John Saunders at Lahore, mistaking him for the superintendent who ordered the lathi charge that killed Lala Lajpat Rai.
whyItMatters: Leads to the Lahore Conspiracy Case trial and the executions of Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, and Sukhdev.

title: Death of Chandrashekhar Azad
summary: Chandrashekhar Azad, surrounded by police at Alfred Park after a tip-off, shoots himself rather than be captured alive.
whyItMatters: Removes the HSRA’s organizing leader weeks before his comrades’ execution.

title: Execution of Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, and Sukhdev
summary: Bhagat Singh, Shivaram Rajguru, and Sukhdev Thapar are hanged at Lahore Central Jail for the assassination of John Saunders.
whyItMatters: Commemorated annually in India as Shaheed Diwas (Martyrs’ Day).
evidenceNote: The sentence specified 24 March; the hanging was moved forward a day to avoid public unrest.

title: Assassination of Michael O’Dwyer
summary: Udham Singh shoots Michael O’Dwyer at a meeting of the East India Association at Caxton Hall, London, twenty-one years after surviving the Jallianwala Bagh massacre that O’Dwyer had approved.
whyItMatters: A direct act of revenge connecting the 1919 Amritsar massacre to events in London two decades later.

title: Execution of Udham Singh
summary: Udham Singh is hanged at Pentonville Prison, London, for the killing of Michael O’Dwyer.
whyItMatters: His remains were repatriated to India in 1974 and he is remembered as "Shaheed-e-Azam."

title: Death of Gopal Krishna Gokhale
summary: Gopal Krishna Gokhale, leading moderate voice of the Indian National Congress, dies at Pune.
whyItMatters: Removes Gandhi’s acknowledged political mentor just as Gandhi returns to India from South Africa.

title: Death of Bal Gangadhar Tilak
summary: Bal Gangadhar Tilak dies at Bombay, on the very date fixed for the launch of Gandhi’s Non-Cooperation Movement.
whyItMatters: Marks a symbolic transition from the earlier generation of nationalist leaders to Gandhi’s mass movement.

title: Annie Besant presides over the Indian National Congress
summary: Annie Besant presides over the Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress, the first woman to hold the office.
whyItMatters: A landmark in women’s leadership of the independence movement.

title: Dharasana Satyagraha
summary: Sarojini Naidu leads around 2,500 volunteers in a nonviolent march on the Dharasana salt works, continuing the Salt Satyagraha after Gandhi’s arrest; police beat the unresisting marchers, drawing international press attention.
whyItMatters: The scenes of unresisting marchers being beaten, reported by American journalist Webb Miller, significantly shifted international opinion against British rule.

title: Dadabhai Naoroji elected to the British Parliament
summary: Dadabhai Naoroji wins the Central Finsbury seat as a Liberal, becoming the first Indian elected to the British House of Commons.
whyItMatters: A landmark in Indian political representation within the British imperial system itself.
evidenceNote: Sources give the date as 5, 6, or 26 July 1892.
